answers.1: The main objects are decimal literals (0.1, 0.2, 0.3) and the double, a 64-bit binary format. A double is a whole number of at most 53 binary digits times a power of two. The other objects are: the stored value (the nearest double to a literal); the gap, meaning the distance between neighbouring doubles, with u = 2^-54 for doubles between 0.25 and 0.5; the error (stored value minus the decimal); the exact sum; the rounded sum; the tie-to-even rule from IEEE 754; the shortest-decimal printing rule; the == comparison; Python's Decimal type; and a tolerance.
answers.2: Each literal is rounded to its stored value, a nearby double. The gap between doubles depends on the size of the number: u/4 near 0.1, u/2 near 0.2 and u near 0.3. So each stored value has its own small error. The + operation adds the stored values exactly, then rounds the result to a double, breaking ties toward an even count of u. == compares the rounded sum with stored 0.3. Printing shows the shortest decimal that rounds back to the same double.
answers.3: 0.1 and 0.2 cannot end in binary, so both are stored slightly too high, while 0.3 is stored slightly too low. Their exact sum lands halfway between two doubles, and the tie rounds up to the double just above stored 0.3, so == is false.
answers.4: The most important variable is whether the decimal's denominator has a factor of 5. If every value is a fraction with a power-of-two denominator, such as 0.5, 0.25 or 0.75, each one is stored with error 0. The exact sum is then itself a double, so == is true. With a factor of 5, the value has to be rounded, and the errors can push the sum onto a different double. The explanation also implies that a larger number has a larger gap, so its rounding error is bigger in absolute terms.
answers.5: Simplification: the sign and exponent bits are left out, and growth of errors over many operations is not covered. Established fact: IEEE 754 rounds a tie to the neighbour with an even count, and stored 0.1 = 0.10000000000000000555.
answers.6: Languages store numbers as doubles: a whole number of up to 53 binary digits times a power of two. 1/10 has a factor of 5 in its denominator, so it repeats forever in binary and must be rounded to the nearest double. As a result, stored 0.1 and 0.2 are slightly high, and stored 0.3 is slightly low. Adding the stored values exactly gives a result halfway between two doubles, and tie-to-even rounds it to the double one gap above stored 0.3, so == is false even though + did its job correctly. Printing shows the shortest decimal that maps back to each double, so 0.1 prints as 0.1 but the sum prints as 0.30000000000000004.
answers.7: The hardest part was counting in units of u (line 23). It does not say why doubles between 0.25 and 0.5 must use whole numbers from 2^52 to 2^53 times 2^-54, rather than a smaller whole number with a larger multiplier. One sentence would help: the whole number always uses all 53 digits. Mixing u/4 steps with values written in u (for example ...198.5) also takes effort.
answers.8: True. 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 have power-of-two denominators, so each is stored exactly. The exact sum, 0.75, is itself a double, so no rounding happens.
answers.9: No. + computes the exact sum of its inputs and rounds it to the nearest double, which is correct. The difference comes from the inputs: they were the stored values, not 0.1 and 0.2. The tie-breaking rounding of the sum then moves the result to a different double from the one 0.3 rounds to.
answers.10: Yes, it is true. Decimal stores base-10 digits, and 1/10 ends in base 10, so all three values are exact.
answers.11: 0.75 = 3 × 2^-2 is a whole number times a power of two. 1/10 has a factor of 5 in its denominator, and no power of two is divisible by 5. So in binary 0.1 repeats forever (0011…) and has to be cut off and rounded.
answers.12: Their errors do not cancel the way 0.3's error needs. Both are rounded up (+5.55e-18 and +1.11e-17), while 0.3 is rounded down (−1.11e-17). The exact sum, ...595.5 u, sits exactly halfway between ...595 and ...596. Tie-to-even sends it to ...596, one gap (5.55e-17) above stored 0.3 at ...595.
answers.13: Printing shows the shortest decimal that rounds back to the same double. The text "0.1" rounds to stored 0.1, so one digit is enough. The sum's double, ...596, needs 0.30000000000000004 instead.
